blurb: How invisible radio waves carry your data, why walls and neighbours slow it down, and what WiFi 6 and 7 really changed.

cards.title: WiFi is just very clever radio

steps.p: Your router and your phone both contain radios. They swap data by sending radio waves — the same kind of energy as FM radio, just at much higher frequencies.
A radio wave is energy that wiggles up and down billions of times a second. WiFi at 2.4 GHz wiggles 2.4 billion times every second.
steps.analogy: Like ripples spreading across a pond, but invisible and incredibly fast.

steps.p: A plain wave carries nothing. Data is added by changing the wave's strength and timing in tiny, precise ways; the receiver reads those changes back as 0s and 1s.

items: Phone reads the changes back as 0s and 1s

steps.p: The router turns radio into wired signals and back. It connects your devices to each other and, through your modem, to the internet.

items: Cable or fibre to the internet

steps.p: WiFi only covers your home. Everything beyond your router travels through cables and fibre.

cards.q: Which radio frequency bands does home WiFi use?
cards.why: 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. These are unlicensed bands anyone may use at low power. Higher frequencies carry more data but fade faster through walls.

cards.title: "Wi-Fi" doesn't stand for anything. "Wireless Fidelity" was invented afterwards.
cards.detail: A branding firm coined the name in 1999 because "IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence" wasn't catchy. The "Wireless Fidelity" tagline was added later and soon dropped.

cards.statement: If your WiFi shows full bars, your internet connection must be fast.
cards.hint: WiFi is only the last few metres.
cards.why: False. Bars only measure the radio link to your router. Your internet connection behind it, or a crowded channel, can still be the bottleneck.

cards.q: Your laptop sends a photo to a printer in the same room over WiFi. Which path does it usually take?
cards.why: Via the router. Devices on a home network talk through the router. The data never needs to leave your home.

cards.statement: WiFi and microwave ovens use roughly the same radio frequency.
cards.why: True. Microwave ovens run near 2.45 GHz, inside WiFi's 2.4 GHz band. A little leakage is why a running microwave can slow nearby 2.4 GHz WiFi.

steps.p: WiFi sets the wave's strength and timing to one of a fixed set of patterns. Each pattern, called a symbol, stands for a few bits.
steps.analogy: Like a set of hand signals: the more signals you know, the more you can say with each one.

steps.p: With 4 patterns, each symbol carries 2 bits. With 1,024 patterns (WiFi 6's 1024-QAM), each carries 10 bits.

visual.caption: Bits per symbol = how many times you can halve the patterns.

steps.h: But only with a clean signal
steps.p: Telling 1,024 patterns apart needs a strong, clean signal. Far from the router, devices fall back to fewer patterns — slower but reliable.
OFDM splits each channel into hundreds of narrow sub-channels sending side by side. Interference ruins only a few, not everything.
On one channel, devices mostly take turns: each listens first, and only talks if the air is quiet.
steps.analogy: Polite people at a dinner party, waiting for a pause before speaking.

cards.q: WiFi 6 can use 1,024 different signal patterns. How many bits does each symbol carry?
cards.hint: 2 multiplied by itself how many times makes 1,024?
cards.why: 10 bits. 2¹⁰ = 1,024, so each pattern can stand for one of 1,024 combinations of 10 bits.

cards.statement: Two laptops on the same WiFi channel can send whenever they like without affecting each other.
cards.why: False. They share the same airwaves, so they take turns. The more busy devices on a channel, the less airtime each gets.

cards.title: Your router announces its network name about ten times every second.
cards.detail: These "beacon" messages, sent roughly every 0.1 seconds by default, announce the name and settings. That's how your phone lists nearby networks.

cards.q: What does MIMO, found in routers with several antennas, let them do?
options: Send separate data streams at once over the same channel
cards.why: Multiple streams. Using several antennas, signals bounce along slightly different paths, and each path can carry its own stream.

cards.q: Why do devices far from the router get slower speeds?
options: Their weaker signal can only tell apart fewer patterns, so each symbol carries fewer bits
Distance uses up the data plan
The router turns them down on purpose to save power
cards.why: Fewer patterns. A noisy signal makes similar patterns hard to tell apart, so the link drops to simpler, slower ones.

steps.p: Travels furthest and through walls best, but is slow and crowded — shared with neighbours, Bluetooth and microwaves.
Faster and with more channels, but shorter range and weaker through walls.
New with WiFi 6E and 7. Lots of clean space and very wide channels, but the shortest range.
Each band is split into channels. In 2.4 GHz, channels overlap, so only 1, 6 and 11 don't interfere with each other.
steps.analogy: Lanes on a motorway: pick a lane nobody else is in.

steps.p: A box saying "AX5400" adds up the maximum speeds of all its bands. No single device ever gets that.

cards.q: In the crowded 2.4 GHz band, which channels are the standard non-overlapping set?
cards.why: 1, 6 and 11. Each 2.4 GHz channel is wide enough to spill onto its neighbours, so these three are spaced far enough apart not to clash.

cards.title: The original 1997 WiFi standard topped out at 2 megabits per second.
cards.detail: That's slower than a basic mobile connection today. Newer generations multiplied speeds with wider channels, denser signal patterns and multiple antennas.

cards.statement: A router sold as "AX5400" will give your laptop 5,400 megabits per second.
cards.why: False. 5,400 is the theoretical total across all bands. One device on one band typically gets a fraction of that.

cards.q: WiFi 6E and WiFi 7 got much of their extra speed from…
options: Access to the 6 GHz band with wider channels
cards.why: The 6 GHz band. Lots of fresh, uncrowded airwaves allow very wide channels, which carry more data.

cards.statement: Higher-frequency WiFi signals generally pass through walls less well than lower-frequency ones.
cards.why: True. That's the trade-off: 6 GHz is fast in the same room, 2.4 GHz still reaches the far bedroom.

steps.p: Signal weakens with distance and with every wall, floor and mirror. Concrete, metal and water (including fish tanks) are especially bad.
Every device on your network — and neighbours on the same channel — takes turns. One slow, distant device can hog airtime.
steps.analogy: One slow talker at a dinner party holding up the conversation.

steps.p: Routers spread signal outward in all directions. Put one in a cupboard in a corner and half its signal is wasted on the outside.
Mesh systems put several linked units around a home, so every room has a strong signal nearby.
Your WiFi password encrypts data only between your device and router. Beyond that, HTTPS protects your connection to websites.

cards.title: A perfectly usable WiFi signal can arrive at less than a billionth of a watt.
cards.detail: A decent reading of −70 dBm equals 0.0000000001 watts. Receivers are extraordinarily good at picking out such faint signals.

cards.q: Where's the best place for a home router?
options: Central and raised, out in the open
On the floor behind the TV
cards.hint: It spreads signal in all directions.
cards.why: Central and high. Signal spreads outward, so the middle of the home reaches every room, and fewer obstacles means stronger signal.

cards.statement: Your WiFi password encrypts your data all the way to the websites you visit.
cards.why: False. It only protects the hop from your device to the router. HTTPS (the padlock) protects the rest of the journey.

cards.q: Which WiFi security setting should you avoid because it can be cracked in minutes?
cards.why: WEP. The original 1999 security has well-known flaws. Use WPA3 if available, otherwise WPA2.

cards.statement: A big fish tank between your router and laptop can weaken the WiFi signal.
cards.why: True. Water absorbs WiFi frequencies well — the same reason microwave ovens heat water.

cards.title: Find your WiFi's weak spots
cards.body: Speed tests in different rooms quickly show where your signal drops off.
cards.challenge: Run a speed test next to your router and in your furthest room. If the gap is huge, try moving the router somewhere more central.
